addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

# custom.md - the project layer

The project's own layer over the pinned agent-files (see
[AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#custommd-the-project-layer)). Loaded last. On conflict, this file wins.

## Medium

The artifact is the `vc-x1` CLI, a Rust crate (manifest `Cargo.toml`, package name `vc-x1`).
Versioning specifics are in [versioning.md](agent-data/versioning.md). The validation commands
are not here: they are the work side's `[validate]` table in `.vc-config.md`, run by
`vc-x1 validate` and `vc-x1 validate --fast`, as the pinned checklists say.

**What a version bump promises**: `X.Y.Z` is a scope signal to readers of the history (see
[Advancing X.Y.Z](agent-data/versioning.md#advancing-xyz-scope-decides)), not a compatibility
contract. The crate has no library target, but the built CLI has external consumers (the family's
repos run it), so a change that breaks an existing invocation or the `.vc-config.md` schema is
called out in the commit and surfaced by the tool's own errors rather than promised by the
version. Revisit with a compat clause if a library crate ever splits out.

**Single-name convention** (adopted at the 0.78.3 cycle): the package name is the binary's
name, `vc-x1` on `main`, with per-line dev names on long-lived branches, guarded by `build.rs`
on every cargo verb. This is the project's answer to versioning.md's
[Dev artifact name](agent-data/versioning.md#dev-artifact-name): the repo is striving to
release, so `main` builds install as plain `vc-x1`. The opening's bump sets the dev name with
the suffixed version, and the closing's bump restores `vc-x1` with the bare one (missed at two
closings before this line was written, 2026-08-22).

## Project conventions and overrides

Project-local conventions, and overrides of the pinned files. An override names the section it
supersedes. A project whose further layer holds these keeps this section empty.

_None._

## Dogfood log

This project's log lives in [notes/dogfood.md](notes/dogfood.md): dated entries on where the
pinned instructions chafed, failed, or got amended, the evidence base for the family's
convergence decisions ([Changing the agent-files](AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)). In-flight
entries only: a resolved entry retires at the beat where it resolves, per
[Retiring Done entries](agent-data/notes.md#retiring-done-entries).

wording, after a fully merged long-lived bookmark was deleted without loss.

## Close-out shapes

The three shapes a cycle can land in, chosen by the user at close-out
([Close-out](../AGENTS.md#close-out)):

- **trapezoid**, the current default: a merge commit whose first parent is the trunk and whose
  second is the ladder, so `git log --first-parent` reads one commit per cycle while every rung
  stays reachable. Reshaped between two pushes by the [recipe below](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe),
  whose last step is `jj git push`, not `vc-x1 push`.
- **keep separate**, one commit per rung on `main`, when the decomposition itself is
  informative.
- **squash** to one commit, right for a focused change. Set up before the close-out push.

## Trapezoid close-out recipe

The commands behind the trapezoid shape in
[Close-out](../AGENTS.md#close-out): a merge commit whose first parent is the trunk line and
whose second parent is the cycle's ladder, published in four steps, an ordinary close-out push,
a two-command reshape, and a second push that re-points the bookmark at the reshaped commit.

```
  main line   ...--<base>------------------<closeout>--
                      \                    /
  ladder             <rung-1>--...--<tip>-+
```

- `<base>`: the **parent of the ladder's first rung**, the trunk position when the cycle
  opened. It becomes the first parent. Not always the previous close-out: a docs interlude
  between cycles sits on the trunk line and must stay there.
- `<tip>`: the cycle's last commit before the close-out. It becomes the second parent.
- `<closeout>`: the close-out commit, created by step 1.

Only step 1 is a `vc-x1 push`. The rest is jj, because after step 1 the commits exist and all
that remains is reshaping and publishing them:

1. `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`: the ordinary close-out push. It
   commits both repos, stamps the `ochid:` trailers, and publishes `<closeout>` linearly.
2. `jj rebase -r <closeout> --onto <base> --onto <tip>`: `<closeout>` becomes the merge.
   Parent order is the argument order.
3. `jj new <closeout>`: an empty `@` above the merge. The bookmark followed the rewrite on its
   own. What step 2 leaves misplaced is the working copy: `jj rebase -r` re-parents descendants
   onto the rebased commit's old parent, so the empty `@` from step 1 lands beside the merge on
   `<tip>` and the tree reverts to pre-close-out content, which looks alarming and is not.
4. `jj git push --bookmark <bookmark> -R .`: publishes the reshaped commit. The agent repo is
   untouched and its session tail goes out with a separate `vc-x1 squash-push` afterwards.

**Step 4 is not a `vc-x1 push`**, learned at a close-out that tried it. Push runs its whole
pipeline or none of it, and by the time the reshape is done `.claude` holds the session writes
from steps 1-3, so `commit-bot` wants to run and the message stage demands a title for it.
Publishing an already-made commit is a different operation from committing and publishing, and
only the latter is push's job.

Details:

- **Verify two parents before step 4.** `jj log -r <closeout> -T 'parents.map(|p|
  p.change_id().short(8))'` must list both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>`
  is an ancestor of `<tip>` (observed at three consecutive close-outs), but a collapsed merge is
  indistinguishable from a correct one in `jj log --no-graph` and is only visible once published.
- **Trailers survive.** The reshape changes `<closeout>`'s SHA but not its change id, so the
  `ochid:` trailers stamped in step 1 stay valid in both directions.
- **Step 4 moves the bookmark sideways.** Step 1's SHA becomes unreachable, so a
  [backfill](../AGENTS.md#commits-backfill) must never read a SHA from the window between the
  two pushes.

- `<tip>`: the cycle's last commit before the close-out. It becomes the second parent.
- `<closeout>`: the close-out commit, created by step 1.

Only step 1 is a `vc-x1 push`. The rest is jj, because after step 1 the commits exist and all
that remains is reshaping and publishing them:

1. `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`: the ordinary close-out push. It
   commits both repos, stamps the `ochid:` trailers, and publishes `<closeout>` linearly.
2. `jj rebase -r <closeout> --onto <base> --onto <tip>`: `<closeout>` becomes the merge.
   Parent order is the argument order.
3. `jj new <closeout>`: an empty `@` above the merge. The bookmark followed the rewrite on its
   own. What step 2 leaves misplaced is the working copy: `jj rebase -r` re-parents descendants
   onto the rebased commit's old parent, so the empty `@` from step 1 lands beside the merge on
   `<tip>` and the tree reverts to pre-close-out content, which looks alarming and is not.
4. `jj git push --bookmark <bookmark> -R .`: publishes the reshaped commit. The agent repo is
   untouched and its session tail goes out with a separate `vc-x1 squash-push` afterwards.

**Step 4 is not a `vc-x1 push`**, learned at a close-out that tried it. Push runs its whole
pipeline or none of it, and by the time the reshape is done `.claude` holds the session writes
from steps 1-3, so `commit-bot` wants to run and the message stage demands a title for it.
Publishing an already-made commit is a different operation from committing and publishing, and
only the latter is push's job.

Details:

- **Verify two parents before step 4.** `jj log -r <closeout> -T 'parents.map(|p|
  p.change_id().short(8))'` must list both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>`
  is an ancestor of `<tip>` (observed at three consecutive close-outs), but a collapsed merge is
  indistinguishable from a correct one in `jj log --no-graph` and is only visible once published.
- **Trailers survive.** The reshape changes `<closeout>`'s SHA but not its change id, so the
  `ochid:` trailers stamped in step 1 stay valid in both directions.
- **Step 4 moves the bookmark sideways.** Step 1's SHA becomes unreachable, so a
  [backfill](../AGENTS.md#commits-backfill) must never read a SHA from the window between the
  two pushes.

Review of the diff, then the rename question.

## Review of your change

**One real defect:** `AGENTS.md:213` has a doubled hash in the anchor:

```
(agent-data/jj.md##trapezoid-close-out-recipe)
```

That link is broken; it needs a single `#`. Two smaller nits on the same line: the label `trapezoid-recipe` is hyphenated where every other inline link in the file uses prose ("recipe below", "Close-out shapes"), and "default" hangs bare after the paren. I would write it as:

```
   - trapezoid, the default ([recipe](agent-data/jj.md#trapezoid-close-out-recipe))
```

The `jj.md` side is fine: moving **squash** to last makes the bullet order match the AGENTS.md list (trapezoid, keep separate, squash), and the AGENTS.md descriptions ("linear series of commits", "single commit") are accurate.

## The rename at landing: one thing to settle first

`custom.md > Single-name convention` currently says the rename back to `vc-x1` is done by the *closing's bump* (in the close-out commit, before the trapezoid recipe's step 1). Your request moves it to landing, which is a different beat, and the trapezoid recipe does not contain the land step at all; landing is `jj.md > Cycle bookmarks: create and land` (`jj bookmark set main -r <bookmark>`, then `jj git push --bookmark main`), and that is a fast-forward of existing commits, so no new content can ride on it.

So "rename at landing" needs a commit to carry the rename, and there are two ways to get one:

1. **Amend it into `<closeout>` during the trapezoid reshape window** (between recipe steps 1 and 4). Step 4 already republishes `<closeout>` under a new SHA with the same change id, so an edit to the manifest there costs nothing extra: add a step "restore the plain name in `Cargo.toml`, `jj squash` it into `<closeout>`" before the verify-two-parents check. This keeps the bookmark holding dev names right up to the reshape, and `main` only ever sees `vc-x1`. Downside: the body of `<closeout>` was written and reviewed before the rename landed in it, and it only works for the trapezoid shape (keep-separate and squash would need their own wording).
2. **Keep the rename in the closing's bump**, as custom.md says now, and leave the recipe alone. The bookmark's tip then already builds as `vc-x1` before landing, which is what "striving to release" implies anyway.

My recommendation is (2) unless the point is that a bookmark tip should still install as `vc-x1-dev` until it is on `main`; in that case (1), and custom.md's sentence about the closing's bump gets rewritten to point at the recipe step. Which do you want? I have not edited anything yet (hard rule 10), and the broken `##` anchor fix is a one-character change I will fold in with whichever you pick.

The plain version: your diff is good except a doubled `##` that breaks the recipe link; the rename-on-landing conflicts with what custom.md says today, and I need you to pick whether the rename rides in the close-out commit (as now) or is squashed in during the trapezoid reshape.

The lead-in reads well now ("Restore the plain name if the project was renamed, otherwise skip:"), and the sub-bullets are consistently unpunctuated. Two notes on the blank-line approach:

1. **It works but has side effects.** In CommonMark a blank line inside any list item makes the *whole* ordered list "loose", so every step 1-5 gets paragraph spacing in renderers that honor it (GitHub does; zed evidently tightens anyway). And `jj.md:242` is not empty, it is three spaces, which is trailing whitespace a formatter or linter will eventually strip, at which point the blank line still works (an empty line is fine) but it is a diff-churn magnet.

content.content:
a body a `--body` flag can mistake for an option.
- **`*` bullets are the problem's facets**: sub-problems that decompose the intro's general
  problem, not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes. A body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is
  usually asking to be more than one commit.
- **`-` bullets are solutions**, and a `-` solves the nearest enclosing problem: nested under a
  `*` facet it solves that facet, at top level it solves the intro's general problem, which is
  how one solution says it retires every facet at once. Position expresses scope.
- **Zero facets is the trivial commit**: a problem paragraph and one or more top-level `-`
  solutions. Not a second form, the general form with an empty middle.

**The markers are typed on purpose**: `*` always means problem, `-` always means solution.
Indentation alone cannot separate them in the trivial case, where a lone top-level `-` reads as a
solution only because `-` always is one. The typing also keeps history greppable (`^\* ` finds
every facet, `^- ` and `^  - ` every solution). Bodies are read as plain text, in `jj log` and in
terminals, where the markers survive, and if a renderer ever flattens them the indentation still
carries the structure. So the mixed markers are deliberate, and a linter's consistent-marker rule
is wrong to normalize them.

Unchanged by this: no version in title or body, no file list, no deliberation, titles per
[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit).

content.content:
manifest. Holding it back is deliberate, buying one timing rule and a record a rebase cannot
  falsify.
- Two headers in one chores file must not share a title, or their anchors collide and the
  duplicate silently resolves to the first. Within a file that is the whole uniqueness
  requirement. Titles may repeat across the repo's history.
- A rung is written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and backfilled in place with a real
  file-local slot once its commit's SHA is permanent (see Timing below).
- Rung citations use the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
  [Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render.
  (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`. The inner `[3]`
  resolves against its `[3]:` definition, and CommonMark / GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The
  `# References` definition puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full
  40-hex SHA** in the title slot:

```
[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
```

- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short, and GitHub / GitLab resolve a unique prefix to
  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
  say) gets the canonical identifier.

**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way, and neither
is its version. A commit can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every rung

content.content:
## The In Progress block

A running cycle's record, `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, written at the opening
([Opening](../AGENTS.md#opening)) and moved to chores at close-out. The picked-up `## Todo`
item is moved here (never copied) and becomes **six provisional items**, all required, all
revised as rungs land. The title is a heading one level below `## In Progress` and the other
five are headings one level below the title (a plain cycle: `###` title, `####` items, and
under a program heading, each one deeper):

- **title**, which becomes the chores section header at close-out
- **problem statement**: what is wrong, a sentence or two
- **solution statement**: what will be done about it, broad. Provisional, and the close-out's
  commit body carries the final one
- **acceptance check**: the measure of "are you finished?", specific enough that a reader can
  run it. Not the per-commit validation, which asks whether the artifact still works. A changed
  check is one of the things the deliberation exists to justify
- **ladder**: one rung per step, `- [[N]] [<title>][M]` plus `(current)` / `(done)`, with
  `[M]: #<slug>` in the file's `# References`. The closing rung, `<cycle title> closing`, is
  linked like the rest
- **deliberation**: how the five above were decided, alternatives weighed, costs accepted.
  `_None._` when there was nothing to deliberate, which is a real answer

A **`Ladder details`** area follows the six: one subsection per rung, the closing included,
headed by the rung's exact title. Each opens at laddering with an abstract-sized intent
statement (the rung's problem and solution in a sentence or two) and completes at the rung's
landing with the conceptual delta: design points, consequences, deferrals, never a restatement
of the landed commit body. The closing rung's opens with the stub "Closing out the cycle." and
completes at close-out with what closing taught, in problem/solution form, or `_None._`.

A rung is `- [[N]] [<title>][M] (marker)` and carries no detail beyond that: the literal
`[[N]]` is the as-built ladder's placeholder, filled only at backfill after landing, and the
title links to the rung's subsection. A step is identified by its title (hard rule 9, prose.md's
[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)), so a title carries no
number and no version. The version-of-record still bumps for every rung and its suffix still
encodes the stage, but that encoding belongs to the manifest and appears nowhere in prose.

Nothing is opened in the chores file while the cycle runs. The block is the cycle's only home
until close-out moves it ([The close-out move](#the-close-out-move)).

## Done entry form

A `## Done` entry (in `TODO.md` and in `done.md`) is the close-out's **version**, then a **bold
title line** carrying its chores `[[N]]` ref, with any detail as sub-bullets:

```
- 0.42.0 **feat: config loader** [[7]]
  - `--config` resolves per-profile pin pools
  - the parse rejects unknown keys rather than ignoring them
```

- **Bold, and detail below rather than beside.** These entries are read by skimming a list for
  one of them, so the title has to be findable without reading the line it sits on. A title
  followed by a paragraph of summary is the wall-of-prose shape
  [Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) warns about, and it hides the one thing a skim is looking
  for. Bold matches the `## In Progress` block, whose title line is already bold.
- **The version leads and the title stays bold**, so the entry answers both questions a reader
  brings: `grep 0.42.0` finds what shipped in a version, and the eye still lands on titles when
  skimming. Putting the version *inside* the bold, or dropping the bold for a plain rung-shaped
  line, trades one of those for the other. See
  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)
  for why a Done entry may carry a version at all when a ladder rung may not.
- **A one-liner is still fine** when the title says it all. The sub-bullets are for when it does
  not. What is not fine is the middle case, a title with sentences trailing off it.
- **Sub-bullets are conceptual, like chores bullets**: what shipped, not a file list, and never
  a copy of the chores intro. The `[[N]]` ref is what carries a reader to the full narrative.
- **Entries written before this convention keep their form** and gain a version when touched. A
  sweep would rewrite history's presentation for no reader's benefit.

## Retiring Done entries

`TODO.md`'s `## Done` section is a rolling buffer of recently shipped work, not a permanent
log. Move entries into `done.md` at these natural beats:

- **Closing a ladder**: when the close-out commit ships, decide which prior entries are no
  longer needed for nearby context and migrate them. The entry form is the same in both files
  (see [Done entry form](#done-entry-form)), so a migration moves the bullet as it stands.
- **Opening a new ladder**: at the opening step, do the same sweep before bumping the
  version-of-record.
- **Resolving an agent-file experiment**: at the beat where it resolves, not at a ladder
  boundary. Adopted and rejected retire identically, since "we tried this and dropped it" is what
  history serves worst. The narrative goes in a `chores-NN.md` section and the dogfood entry is
  removed from wherever the project keeps its log, so that log carries in-flight entries only. See
  [Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files).

Migration mechanics:

- Move the bullet itself from `TODO.md > ## Done` to `done.md` (preserving the original ref
  number).
- Copy any references the moved entries cite into `done.md`'s `# References` section (those
  refs are file-local, so coexisting with `TODO.md`'s namespace is fine).
- Prune any references in `TODO.md > # References` no longer cited by anything in
  `## In Progress` / `## Todo` / `## Done`. This frees the numbers for future reuse.

753:## Done
## Done

Completed tasks are moved from `## Todo` to here, `## Done`, as they are completed
and older `## Done` sections are moved to [done.md](notes/done.md) to keep this file small.

_Migrated to [done.md](notes/done.md) on 2026-07-24 (the DRY jj facade
cycle and its two docs interludes: template repo names, notes rework)._

- 0.80.2 **docs: halve AGENTS.md into rationale.md** [[59]]
  - AGENTS.md 593 to 340 lines: the why in the new pinned `agent-data/rationale.md`, headings
    mirroring AGENTS.md's, the restated mechanics in the satellites that own them, the rule
    text tightened twice (the agent's pass, then wink's, item by item)
  - two rules added: backfill is the Opening's first step with its `rg` check, and a list
    lead is an unmarked label ending in a colon (prose.md)
  - rules changed at wink's pass: repos always hyphenated, Bump before Work, push expected at
    every rung, both repos' commits share title and body
  - filed: `validate --full`, the validate element for unfilled rungs, the satellites' why-move

- 0.80.1 **docs: fold the cycle agent-files into AGENTS.md** [[29]]
  - `AGENTS.md` holds the cycle protocol as `## Cycle protocol`, one account in the order a
    cycle meets it, with the at-rest contract (agent pushes, agent stops, user squash-pushes
    the agent repo) stated once, and `cycle-protocol.md` and `cycle-checklists.md` are gone,
    their jj mechanics (trapezoid recipe, local-ladder moves) in jj.md
  - "Ladder (sub-cycle)" retired for "local ladder", "bot repo" for "agent repo" with the
    actor now "the agent", the "Work" stage name retired, and the Cycle term simplified to
    one change run from opening to closing as one commit or a ladder of them
  - filed the next convention cycle: halve AGENTS.md by moving its rationale into
    `agent-data/rationale.md`
  - dissolves the Todos "Shared-doc sync: As-built ladder rungs carry `[[N]]` commit refs"
    and "Shared-doc sync: per-commit chores convention": both conventions are pinned in
    AGENTS.md and the sync they asked for is the convergence model, and files the backlog
    entry "Sweep the Todo files for pre-0.80 names and retired conventions"

- 0.80.0 **docs: empty custom-family into the pinned set and config** [[58]]
  - the agent side is `agent` in config (`repos.agent`, `[agent-session]`), on the CLI
    (`--scope=agent`, `agent-session`, `validate-agent`), and in the schema's homes, the old
    spellings rejected with fix-its
  - the family facts and the validation commands moved from `custom-family.md` into
    work-side `[family]` and `[validate]` tables, the latter a new `str-list` kind the TOML
    reader learned arrays for
  - `vc-x1 validate [--fast]` runs the configured table, one invocation per element,
    stopping at the first failure, and the pinned checklists name it
  - the messaging behavior is pinned in `agent-data/messaging.md`, `custom.md` holds the
    medium prose alone, and `custom-family.md` is gone
  - a breaking config change for the family: install 0.80.0 first, then respell, since a
    0.79.x binary reads a respelled config as single-repo, silently

pin two rules and close the convergence record)._

agent-file set, three semicolons, line widths, freshen vc-config, the depth-note paragraph,
and the refactor program block)._

_Migrated to [done.md](notes/done.md) on 2026-08-18 (the three pre-convention entries: the
typeable-punctuation source sweep, drop sync state, and the Claude Code cycle test)._

_Migrated to [done.md](notes/done.md) on 2026-08-09 (the
jj-lib migration and 0.43-bump cycles, and the three docs
interludes: jj-lib design notes, typeable punctuation,
re-describe rule)._

_Migrated to [done.md](notes/done.md) on 2026-08-03 (the
program-ladder, repo-registry, trapezoid-recipe, and
stateless-push entries), and on 2026-07-28 (the

152:## Suffix scheme
153-
154-The cycle (opening -> commits -> closing, per the
155-[Cycle protocol](../AGENTS.md#cycle-protocol)) encodes each commit's phase in the version
156-suffix, the **final identifier `0` marking a Preparation**.
157-
158-This is the manifest's own spelling, read by whoever inspects `Cargo.toml` or `-V` output. It is
159-not a name for a step: a step is identified by its title, and an in-flight ladder rung carries
160-neither a number nor a version (see
161-[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). The one
162-prose surface that records a version is a chores as-built rung, where it is a property of a landed
163-commit sitting beside that commit's SHA. The identifiers below count commits within a phase, and
164-nothing dereferences one.
165-
166-- `X.Y.Z-0`: Preparation
167-- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...: the commits between
168-- `X.Y.Z`: Close-out (bare version, no suffix)
169-
170-**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle, with no ladder and no setup commit, skips `-0`
171-and starts at `-1` (its first commit). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle needing no
172-Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that grows a Preparation later adds the `0` step
173-without renumbering siblings.
174-
175-Disambiguation:
176-
177-- `-10`: commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a Preparation.
178-- `-1.0`: Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final identifier `0`).
179-
180-**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:
181-
182-- `X.Y.Z-3.0`: Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle

What I was thinking was tweaks was going to be a single-step commit, so for that case, pretending I'd changed some code in tweaks and had compiled, we just:
- `jj bookmark set tweaks -r @`
- `jj new main` or `jj edit main`
- `vc-x1 validate --fast` to install the "real" vc-x1
- `jj new tweaks`
- Update cargo.toml to be vc-x1-dev and version 0.80-3
- and do whatever else on tweaks eventually merging as a single-step or multi-setup trapezoid ...

content.text:
Approximately, with four corrections:

1. **`jj new main`, never `jj edit main`.** `main` is immutable in jj, so `jj edit main` refuses (and with `--ignore-immutable` it would put your working copy *inside* the landed commit). `jj new main` gives an empty `@` on `main`, which is what you want.

2. **The reinstall needs the full `vc-x1 validate`, not `--fast`.** `--fast` runs only `cargo test --bins`; the `cargo install` step that replaced `~/.cargo/bin/vc-x1` earlier is in the full table.

3. **`jj edit tweaks` rather than `jj new tweaks` for a single-step cycle.** `vc-x1 push` commits `@` only. `jj new tweaks` puts the manifest edits in an empty child, leaving `tweaks` itself as an undescribed change below it that push never touches, so you would need a `jj squash` before the push. `jj edit tweaks` keeps everything in the one change that becomes the commit. (`jj new tweaks` is right for a multi-step cycle, where `tweaks` would be squashed into the rungs it belongs to.)

4. **The version and name depend on when.** While iterating on `tweaks`, `vc-x1-dev 0.80.3-1` (a lightweight cycle skips `-0` and starts at `-1`), so every `validate` installs the dev binary. At the moment of the single push, which is the close-out, the rules say bare `0.80.3` and plain `vc-x1`, because the one commit is landing on `main` and the guard allows bare-with-plain. The Opening's Rename step and the recipe's restore step collapse into the same commit, which is why a single-step cycle never shows `vc-x1-dev` in history.

The rest of the Opening still applies to a single-step cycle: backfill check, publish the bookmark (ideally named by the title's slug), the In Progress block, the sweep. The close-out move and Done entry ride in the same commit. If the cycle later grows a second step, bump the first commit to `-1` in your head, leave it as-is in history, and the next rung is `-2`.

message.content: Your thoughts on ss (single-step) vs ms (multi-step)?

content.text:
For this cycle: multi-step, and the reason is the cycle's own subject. The rule being added is "rename at the opening, restore at close-out", and a single-step cycle collapses both into one commit, so the history would never show `vc-x1-dev` and the acceptance check's first line ("`vc-x1-dev` on every rung of the bookmark") would have nothing to check. The ms run is the only way this cycle exercises what it writes, and the opening has already done half of it (`vc-x1-dev 0.80.3-0` is installed beside `vc-x1 0.80.2`).

I would trim the ladder by one, though. The relink rung is a one-line link plus a bullet reorder in the same two files the recipe rung touches, so folding it in costs nothing in reviewability. The commit-body cue stays its own rung, since it is a different rule with a different why. That gives four commits: opening, recipe rung (rename step, restore step, relink, the two semicolons), cue rung, closing.

The general rule I would apply going forward:

- **ss** when the change is one reviewable diff, nothing installs mid-cycle, and the opening bookkeeping is light. Most docs fixes and one-file bug fixes. The bookmark still exists, so review and landing are unchanged, and the dev name is never needed because the one commit is the close-out.
- **ms** when the diff wants reviewing in sittings, when the binary changes mid-cycle (so a dev install matters), or when two rule changes should each be greppable on their own. Anything that touches code and docs together is usually ms.

The cost of ms is one review stop per rung, which is exactly the thing the tiers in Policy let you delegate when the rungs are mechanical.

If you agree, I will drop the relink rung from the block (ladder and its subsection) before the opening push. The working copy is otherwise unchanged and awaiting your review.

Mine sorted by file type, yours by whether an intermediate state has to exist: a cycle is ms when some rung needs to be built and exercised on its own before the next rung makes sense, or when the diff wants reviewing in pieces. One cohesive change, however many kinds of file it touches, is ss. The dev name falls straight out of that: it exists to protect the released binary *during* the mid-cycle installs that make a cycle ms in the first place.

Where to capture it: AGENTS.md's Terminology already ends the Cycle definition with "A cycle is single-step or multi-step", which names the two without saying how to choose. One sentence after it would do:

> Single-step when the change is one cohesive, reviewable diff, whatever files it touches. Multi-step when an intermediate state has to be installed to verify it, or the diff wants reviewing in sittings, so the dev name and the per-rung stops earn their cost.

The why goes in rationale.md under the mirrored heading, per the pattern.

Mechanically this is a rule change meant for the family, and this is a convention cycle, so it rides as its own rung rather than an inserted one. Proposed ladder, with the relink rung folded into the recipe rung as discussed:

- opening (current)
- docs: rename at the opening and restore in the trapezoid recipe
- docs: cue the commit-body form at the describe step
- docs: say when a cycle is single-step or multi-step
- closing

Say go and I will reshape the block (ladder, the two subsections) before the opening push, which is still waiting on your review.

message.content: My ss vs ms: "If the initial problem statement has a straight forward coding solution step with only documentation as other steps, this is a good candidate for single-step, otherwise assume multi-step which can always be squashed into a single-step." Thoughts

content.text:
The default flip is the strong part: assume ms, and let the squash close-out shape collapse it. That asymmetry is real, since an ms cycle squashes into one commit at close-out with no loss, while an ss cycle that turns out to need a second step has to grow a ladder mid-flight, bump its first commit's meaning, and cannot get the dev-name protection back for the install it already did. So the safe error is ms, and the rule should say so, as yours does.

Two wording points:

1. "with only documentation as other steps" reads as if docs are always separate steps, and it excludes a docs-only cycle (this one would not qualify as ss under it, though a one-sentence docs fix should). I would phrase the ss side as "one straightforward solution step, its documentation riding in the same commit", which covers code-plus-docs and docs-only alike.
2. "can always be squashed" is true at close-out via the squash shape, but the rung pushes to the bookmark still happened, so the cost ms pays (a review stop per rung) is not recovered by squashing. Worth saying that is the price, so the default is chosen knowingly.

Proposed sentence for Terminology, after "A cycle is single-step or multi-step":

> Single-step when the problem statement has one straightforward solution step, its documentation riding in the same commit. Otherwise assume multi-step, which the squash close-out shape can always collapse to one commit, while a single-step cycle cannot grow a ladder after its install.

The why (the asymmetry) goes in rationale.md under the mirrored heading. Same plan as before for the rung: it rides as "docs: say when a cycle is single-step or multi-step" after the cue rung. The opening is still waiting on your review, with the ladder reshape to do first on your go.

message.content: "while a single-step cycle cannot grow a ladder after its install", I don't think so, if we assume the default is "always" a "bookmark/branch" with -dev name. As the owners and sole users of this app at this time we'll sometimes cheat but the general rule is development is not done on main.

content.text:
You are right, and the correction sharpens the rule rather than weakening it. My clause assumed the ss commit had already gone out under the plain name. Under "always a bookmark, always `-dev` while iterating", an ss cycle is just an ms cycle whose ladder happens to have one rung: up to the push nothing is committed, so it grows a second rung for free, and even after a push the bookmark is mutable, so the first commit can be re-suffixed with the usual coordination. The dev name is what makes that true, which is a better argument for the rename step than anything I wrote earlier.

So the rule reduces to your default plus the one ss shape, and the asymmetry is only about cost, not possibility. Proposed sentence for Terminology, after "A cycle is single-step or multi-step":

> Single-step when the problem statement has one straightforward solution step, its documentation riding in the same commit. Otherwise assume multi-step: development runs on the bookmark under the dev name either way, so a single-step cycle grows a ladder at no cost, and the squash close-out shape collapses a multi-step one to one commit.

And "development is not done on `main`" is worth stating as a sentence of its own in "Cycles run on a bookmark", since rule 13 implies it without saying it, and the docs-interlude sentence in the recipe contradicts it. I would fold that into the same rung, with the recipe sentence reworded to match.

The opening is still waiting on your review, with the ladder reshape (fold relink into the recipe rung, add the ss/ms rung) to do first on your go.

content.text:
Two things, one mine and one zed's.

**Mine.** The script that reshaped the Problem section took the slice between `t.index("#### Problem\n\nThe single-name convention")` and `t.index("#### Solution\n")`. The second search had no start bound, so it matched the `#### Solution` in the In Progress *template* block at the top of the file, which sits about 40 lines *before* the real one. End before start gives an empty slice, and `str.replace("", new)` in Python inserts `new` at every character boundary. 52 KB of file times a 900-byte insert is the 41 MB you saw. My redo passed the start index as the second argument to `index` and asserted the slice was non-empty.

**Zed's.** Zed watches the working tree and reloads a changed file's buffer. A 41 MB markdown file is not pathological on its own, but the way I corrupted it was: 52 thousand copies of the same 15-line block, so tree-sitter's markdown grammar got 52 thousand headings and bullet lists to parse and the highlighter a matching number of nodes, on top of the rope and the undo history for a reload-sized edit. It reached 12.5 GB resident and was still grinding when you killed it. The `zed .` hang was downstream: the CLI only hands the path to the running instance over its socket (`zed-cli:///tmp/.tmp5tILqk/socket` in your `ps`), so with that instance wedged the CLI waited forever.

The net: nothing in either repo was harmed. The bad version lived on disk for about a minute and in one jj operation snapshot, and `TODO.md` on disk and in `@` is the good 52 KB version, validated.

The plain version: I built a bad string and wrote it, zed faithfully tried to display it and ran out of patience, killing zed was the right fix and nothing was lost.

Let me separate the two, because I think they have one root.

**What I got wrong.** The opening commit's body restated the *cycle's* problem (the four gaps) and then bolted the opening's own work on as facets. A commit body describes what *that commit* resolves. The opening resolves "the cycle is not set up": unfilled rungs, a stale Done buffer, no In Progress block, manifest on the released version. The four gaps belong to the In Progress block and the closing commit, not here. That is also why you counted six: four gaps in the intro plus two facets reads as six problems for a four-rung ladder. My first draft today made the same move in the other direction, describing the whole cycle in a single commit. So the consistent mistake is scope, not markers: I keep writing the cycle's problem where the commit's belongs. The markers were per prose.md (`*` facet, `-` solution), but if they read as wrong to you, that is a signal about the form, which brings me to the second point.

**Suggestions for the form.** Two changes, either alone helps, together I think they fix it:

1. *Scope sentence in the rule.* Commit-body form says the intro "states the general problem" and never says whose. Add: "the problem this commit resolves, never the cycle's, which lives in the In Progress block and the closing commit's body". For a rung that is the one-line fix. A corollary worth stating: a body whose problem count exceeds the commit's diff is describing something bigger than the commit.

2. *Labels instead of typed markers.* The `*` / `-` typing asks the reader to remember a convention that no other Markdown uses, and it let me produce a structurally valid body that was wrong. Explicit labels are unmistakable and greppable:

   Problem: the cycle is not set up. The halve cycle's ten as-built rungs

   Solution: backfill the rungs with versions and SHAs, sweep 0.80.0 to
   done.md, write the In Progress block with one rung per gap, and take

2. **Bookend bodies are pointers.** Your draft is right that an opening solves nothing, so the problem/solution shape has nothing to hold. content.content:
## Terminology

**Rationale.** The headings mirror so that a missing entry is a grep away: a rule's why is
either at its own slug or nowhere, and nothing has to be searched for by wording. The file
exists so the argument can leave AGENTS.md without dying: a session needs the rule, whoever
would change the rule needs the argument, and a rule whose cost is not written down is the one
an editor simplifies away. Filed as the Todo "Halve AGENTS.md: move its rationale into
`agent-data/rationale.md`" (wink, 2026-08-21).

**Retired names.** "Bot repo" (2026-08-21), when the code respelled the side `agent`.
"Instruction files", which named the agent-files back when `custom.md` was the only editable
one. "Ladder (sub-cycle)" for a local ladder, under [Local ladders](#local-ladders).

**Agent-files** is always hyphenated because it names one set rather than a two-word noun
phrase, and it matches its sibling directory `agent-data/`. **`custom.md` is never pinned**
because holding what the pinned files structurally cannot is its job. **Project layer** is
called a *layer* because it loads last and wins conflicts, so it sits over the pinned set
rather than beside it.

## The dual-repo model
---
### Cycles run on a bookmark

A cycle that pushes `main` directly makes every correction a coordinated force-push of
published history. Landing costs one command and buys free rewrites for the whole cycle. A
single-step cycle gets a bookmark for the same reason: a one-commit line is exactly where a
pre-landing rewrite is cheapest.

Pushing to the bookmark makes the work durable and visible, but landing on `main` is
publication, and that is the line the rules divide at. The series is kept self-consistent
before landing so the branch reads as one coherent ladder. Amending content rather than
re-describing keeps hard rule 4 intact and lets the `ochid:` trailers ride along: they carry
change ids, which survive a rewrite.

### Opening
---

- `<base>`: the **parent of the ladder's first rung**, the trunk position when the cycle
  opened. It becomes the first parent. Not always the previous close-out: a docs interlude
  between cycles sits on the trunk line and must stay there.
- `<tip>`: the cycle's last commit before the close-out. It becomes the second parent.
- `<closeout>`: the close-out commit, created by step 1.

### Commit-body form

A commit body is the [Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape) with one addition: a body whose
problem has several sub-problems arranges them by a fixed recursion, so a reader knows what any
bullet is from its marker and its depth. The earlier statement, "a problem statement then a
solution statement, both broad", left that arrangement to taste, and taste converged slowly and
separately.

- **An intro paragraph states the general problem**, and defines any word the title assumes. It
  is mandatory. [Prose form](#prose-form) wants it regardless, and a body opening on a bullet is
  a body a `--body` flag can mistake for an option.
- **`*` bullets are the problem's facets**: sub-problems that decompose the intro's general
  problem, not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes. A body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is
  usually asking to be more than one commit.
- **`-` bullets are solutions**, and a `-` solves the nearest enclosing problem: nested under a
  `*` facet it solves that facet, at top level it solves the intro's general problem, which is
  how one solution says it retires every facet at once. Position expresses scope.
- **Zero facets is the trivial commit**: a problem paragraph and one or more top-level `-`
  solutions. Not a second form, the general form with an empty middle.

**The markers are typed on purpose**: `*` always means problem, `-` always means solution.
Indentation alone cannot separate them in the trivial case, where a lone top-level `-` reads as a
solution only because `-` always is one. The typing also keeps history greppable (`^\* ` finds
every facet, `^- ` and `^  - ` every solution). Bodies are read as plain text, in `jj log` and in
terminals, where the markers survive, and if a renderer ever flattens them the indentation still
carries the structure. So the mixed markers are deliberate, and a linter's consistent-marker rule
is wrong to normalize them.

content.text:
Correct, and for the reason you gave: "Diff marked commit -> this" is a tree-to-tree diff (`git diff <mark> <this>`), and a squash of a range is by definition the tree at the end against the tree at the start. Commits in between, and the shape they are in, do not enter into it. So marking `<base>` (the parent of the opening) and diffing to `<closeout>` (the merge) shows exactly what the cycle would look like squashed to one commit, which is also exactly what `git log --first-parent -p` will show for that merge, since `<base>` is its first parent.

Two refinements:

- In the trapezoid the mark does not even need to be chosen by hand: `<closeout>^1` *is* `<base>`, so "diff this commit against its first parent" gives the same view, and `git show --first-parent <closeout>` prints it at the command line. The jj spelling is `jj diff --from <base> --to <closeout>`.
- The caveat is the one you identified: the mark is excluded, so the mark must be the commit *before* the opening, not the opening. Mark the opening and the diff drops everything the opening did (the backfill, the sweep, the `-dev` rename).

One thing the trick is good for beyond review: it is the same diff that lands on `main` when the bookmark is fast-forwarded, so what you see there is what `main` will carry, the restored `vc-x1` name included once recipe step 2 has been squashed into `<closeout>`.

message.content: Bottom line we can make a linear or trapezoidal commit in our branch and easily see "how big" and the exact contents to help deciding if we want to squash or not.

content.text:
Yes. The squash decision is "is the net diff one readable change, or does the decomposition carry information?", and the mark-diff answers the first half directly: the size is visible in the stat, the contents in the diff. If the net diff reads cleanly on its own, squash loses nothing; if it reads as several changes stacked, the trapezoid keeps each rung reachable while `--first-parent` still shows the same net view. Either way the choice is made on what `main` will actually carry, not on a guess.

That would be a useful sentence in jj.md's Close-out shapes, since today the section names the three shapes without saying how to look before choosing. One line: "To see what a squash would carry, diff `<base>` to the tip (`jj diff --from <base> --to <tip>`, or gitk's mark-and-diff)." It is a rule change meant for the family, so it would ride as a backlog entry or a small rung of its own rather than be slipped into the closing. Want it filed as a Todo, or added to this cycle as a rung before the closing?

message.content: The "nice" thing in gitk I can increase "Lines of context" to get more context and if it's a large number like 1000 (i.e. as large as the largest file) you can see the "entire context"!

content.text:
That is a good trick: at full context the diff view becomes the file itself with the changes marked in place, which is the closest thing to reading the result rather than the edit. It suits the agent-files especially, where a one-line rule change only makes sense against the paragraph around it. The command-line equivalents are `git diff -U1000` and `jj diff --context 1000`, for the same effect in a terminal.

It also answers the review half of the squash question: at full context you are reading what `main` will carry, section by section, which is the review that matters at landing.
